source.title: Labeling Neural Representations with Inverse Recognition
source.authors: Kirill Bykov; Laura Kopf; Shinichi Nakajima; Marius Kloft; M. Höhne

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures how well neural representations align with labeled concepts and compares explanation metrics, but it does not test whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs or whether those responses count as polysemanticity.
record.gate_note: The reported neuron-to-concept scores and comparisons concern explanation quality, not the prevalence or classification of polysemantic neurons. The numeric correlations below are recorded as related findings that fit none of the claim versions.
record.test_reason: INVERT is a neuron-labelling method. Its results are explanation accuracy, metric comparisons (IoU vs AUC), cost and applications. It never measures, counts or classifies polysemantic neurons, and it does not use polysemanticity as a tool. The only link to the originals is a citation of Zoom In in the related-work section. The IoU-vs-AUC comparison concerns how explanations are scored, but never whether a neuron counts as polysemantic, so it does not test V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that INVERT links neurons to compositional concepts using AUC, without segmentation masks, at lower cost. It adds a statistical significance test and is useful for finding spurious correlations, explaining circuits and handcrafting circuits. They make no claim about polysemanticity.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes INVERT, which searches for concepts using AUC similarity and beam search; it does not reproduce the methods in the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Explanation AUC and concept fraction vary with formula length and the minimum concept-fraction parameter α; IoU and AUC scores are not strongly aligned.

fits_no_version.finding: IoU and AUC neuron-concept scores correlate only weakly and positively (about 0.21–0.41) for non-zero-IoU concepts in Places365 ResNet18 and DenseNet161 layers. The best explanation under one metric does not maximise the other.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron-to-concept explanation metrics (IoU vs AUC) are only weakly aligned, so the label assigned to a neuron depends on the scoring metric.

fits_no_version.finding: Simplicity-precision tradeoff: neurons get their highest AUC for a single narrow class. Broader compositional explanations lower AUC (Figure 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Broader (compositional) neuron explanations trade off against precision of fit.

record.problems: The study does not measure polysemanticity or report how many neurons respond to unrelated concepts. Some explanation comparisons are presented in figures rather than numerical tables.
record.rows_left_out: Results in Table 4 and Figures 4, 11, and 12 compare explanation metrics, concept fractions, and explanation settings, but do not report polysemanticity outcomes; they were not entered as rows for the claim versions.

untested.parts: Whether vision neurons respond to several unrelated inputs. Neurons are labelled with compositional concepts, but mixtures are never assessed as unrelated.
All of it: no language models are studied.
All of it. Several architectures are explained, but no polysemanticity share is compared across them.
Whether the activation range examined or the scoring method changes polysemantic classification. IoU vs AUC disagreement is shown only for single-label explanation quality.

record.verdict_notes: The relation was changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': the text never mentions polysemanticity or superposition. Table 5 'Log' correlation columns are also unrecorded, but they bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Whether vision neurons respond to several unrelated inputs.
Language-model MLP neurons and their responses to unrelated tokens or contexts.
Effects of activation function, architecture, or regularization on polysemanticity.
Whether apparent polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or related jobs.
Whether activation range or explanation scoring changes which neurons count as polysemantic.
